final_diagnosis.text: Miliary tuberculosis with repeatedly negative initial microbiological tests, mistaken for sarcoidosis on non-necrotising granulomas, treated with high-dose steroid and complicated by secondary haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis

final_dx.text: Miliary tuberculosis with repeatedly negative initial microbiological tests, mistaken for sarcoidosis on non-necrotising granulomas, treated with high-dose steroid and complicated by secondary haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis

secondary_findings: Secondary haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (DX.HLH, ICD-10 D76.1), triggered by the tuberculosis (fever, cytopenias, ferritin 7821 ug/L, soluble IL-2 receptor 7593 ng/L, CXCL9 52 784 ng/L, marrow haemophagocytes; H-score 256); scored through the rubric, not as a final-diagnosis id
Acute hypoxic respiratory failure and shock from day 18 (acute respiratory distress syndrome suspected)
accepted_differential: Haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis from another trigger (EBV, lymphoma)
red_herrings: Negative sputum AFB smears, MTB PCR and mycobacterial cultures
Negative first cell-free DNA and pathogen sequencing
Non-necrotising (non-caseating) granulomas in the lung and marrow
key_discriminators: Random miliary nodules with four months of fever, cough, night sweats and weight loss
The low sensitivity of every single TB test in miliary disease
No response to high-dose steroid, then worsening
Pancytopenia with rising ferritin and transaminases (secondary haemophagocytosis)
Repeat sequencing and second lavage AFB stain and PCR positive on day 25
teaching_points: In miliary disease a negative IGRA, smear, PCR, culture or even cell-free DNA sequencing does not exclude tuberculosis; pretest probability should drive empirical treatment.
Non-necrotising granulomas do not separate tuberculosis from sarcoidosis; sarcoidosis is a diagnosis of exclusion.
Never start high-dose steroid for presumed sarcoidosis without cover when miliary tuberculosis is still possible.
In secondary haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, treating the trigger is the only intervention clearly linked to survival.
treatment_given: High-dose steroid for presumed sarcoidosis (curator's day 7); then dexamethasone and etoposide (HLH-2004, day 15); empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics and antifungals, intubation and vasopressors from day 18; rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol from day 25 with HLH chemotherapy withheld.
outcome: Multi-organ failure; died about one week after starting anti-tuberculosis treatment. Autopsy declined, so whether tuberculosis was present from the start or reactivated under immunosuppression is not proven; the authors think it was present from the start, and the case follows them.

must_do.text: Keep tuberculosis high on the list despite negative tests, given the miliary pattern, the symptoms and the origin
Start empirical anti-tuberculosis treatment when suspicion stays high despite negative tests, and before or with any steroid
Send samples from more than one site (sputum and lavage, marrow, urine, blood or liver) for AFB stain, MTB PCR and mycobacterial culture, and repeat testing when the course changes
Recognise secondary haemophagocytosis (cytopenias, ferritin, triglycerides, fibrinogen, soluble IL-2 receptor, marrow) and treat its trigger
Isolate the patient while tuberculosis is possible and involve infectious diseases early
Notify public health and arrange screening of household contacts

must_not_do.text: Diagnose sarcoidosis and start high-dose steroid without anti-tuberculosis cover while miliary tuberculosis has not been reliably excluded
Treat haemophagocytosis with etoposide or escalating immunosuppression without treating the trigger
Take a negative interferon-gamma release assay, smears or sequencing as excluding miliary tuberculosis and commit to sarcoidosis

diagnosis_rubric_anchors.5: Miliary (disseminated) tuberculosis with secondary haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis recognised
diagnosis_rubric_anchors.4: Miliary or other tuberculosis without recognising the haemophagocytosis, or haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis with tuberculosis named as its trigger
diagnosis_rubric_anchors.3: Another disseminated granulomatous infection (non-tuberculous mycobacteria, histoplasmosis)
diagnosis_rubric_anchors.2: Sarcoidosis, lymphoma or haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis without its trigger
diagnosis_rubric_anchors.1: Unrelated diagnosis, or one that would lead to harm
